entries.short: The regulator-approved reference text for prescribers: what a medicine is approved for, how to use it, and its risks.
entries.simpler: Think of it as the medicine's official user manual for doctors. If anything else disagrees, the manual wins.

example.text: Januvia's EU SmPC is the anchor of the sitagliptin module; its section 4.1 lists every approved use.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the PIL: the PIL is the plain-language leaflet for patients, written from the SmPC.

entries.short: The plain-language leaflet in the box, written for patients and based on the SmPC.
entries.simpler: The SmPC is the technical manual; the PIL is the quick-start guide written for the person taking the medicine.

example.text: Vazkepa's PIL says breastfeeding is 'not recommended', while the SmPC says to weigh benefit and risk. The SmPC is the reference.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the SmPC. When the two differ, the SmPC wins.

entries.short: The EMA's published evaluation of a medicine authorised through the EU-wide (centralised) procedure.
entries.simpler: It's the examiner's marking notes, published: what the assessors saw, liked and doubted.

example.text: Januvia's EPAR records that non-inferiority against glipizide was 'not convincingly' shown because the glipizide dose was low.

entries.notToConfuse: Medicines approved country by country (e.g. Crestor, Secalip Supra) have no EPAR; they have national assessment reports instead.

entries.short: The company legally responsible for a medicine in a given market.
entries.simpler: The name on the licence: the company that answers to the regulator if something goes wrong.

example.text: Vazkepa's MAH changed from Amarin to Recordati after their 2025 licensing deal.

entries.notToConfuse: Not necessarily the manufacturer or the local distributor; those can be other companies.

translations.fr: titulaire de l'autorisation de mise sur le marché (AMM)

entries.short: One EMA assessment leading to a single licence valid in every EU member state.
entries.simpler: One exam, one certificate, valid in the whole EU.

example.text: Forxiga went through the centralised procedure in 2012, so it has one EU SmPC and a full EPAR.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the mutual recognition procedure, where one country assesses and others are asked to recognise it.

entries.short: One EU country assesses a medicine first; other countries are asked to recognise that approval.
entries.simpler: One teacher marks the exam, and other schools decide whether to accept the grade.

example.text: Crestor was first approved in the Netherlands in 2002; Spain withdrew from the 2003 recognition round and only authorised it in 2008.

entries.notToConfuse: Not centralised: there is no single EU licence and no EPAR.

entries.short: A formal EU-wide review of a medicine or class, triggered by a safety, efficacy or disagreement question.
entries.simpler: Calling in the referee when countries disagree or a new concern appears.

example.text: The 2009–2011 Article 31 referral moved fibrates to second-line, but kept fenofibrate's add-on-to-statin use.

entries.notToConfuse: The article number matters: 31 = public-health concern; 29 = disagreement during mutual recognition; 20 = centrally authorised medicines.

entries.short: A copy of an off-patent medicine, authorised because it behaves the same in the body as the original.
entries.simpler: Same recipe, different bakery, proven to rise the same way.

example.text: Dapagliflozin Viatris was authorised as a generic of Forxiga after showing bioequivalence.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a biosimilar (for biological medicines), and not a different salt or strength with its own trials.

entries.short: Blood levels of a copy are close enough to the original's that they count as the same medicine.
entries.simpler: Two kettles that boil the same water in the same time: the details inside differ, the result doesn't.

example.text: Sitagliptin SUN showed bioequivalence with Januvia 100 mg; the 25 and 50 mg strengths got a biowaiver.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a clinical outcome trial: it compares blood levels, not heart attacks.

entries.short: Two or more medicines in one tablet or capsule.
entries.simpler: A two-in-one shampoo: fewer bottles, but you can't adjust each ingredient separately.

example.text: Nustendi combines bempedoic acid 180 mg and ezetimibe 10 mg in one tablet.

entries.notToConfuse: Not co-administration, which means taking separate tablets together.

entries.short: Any ingredient in a tablet or capsule other than the active substance.
entries.simpler: The packaging and glue of the pill, not the medicine itself, but some people react to it.

example.text: Vazkepa's sorbitol and maltitol mean people with hereditary fructose intolerance shouldn't take it.

entries.notToConfuse: Not 'inactive' in every sense: excipients like lactose, soya or sorbitol can matter for some patients.

entries.short: The condition and patient group a medicine is officially approved to treat (SmPC section 4.1).
entries.simpler: The job description the regulator signed off.

example.text: Vazkepa's single indication: statin-treated, high-risk adults with triglycerides ≥1.7 mmol/L.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a guideline recommendation: guidelines advise practice; the indication is what the licence allows.

entries.short: A situation in which a medicine must not be used.
entries.simpler: A 'Do not enter' sign, as opposed to 'Drive carefully'.

example.text: Januvia's only contraindication is allergy; pregnancy is 'should not be used', a weaker category.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a warning or precaution ('use with care'), and not 'should not be used'.

entries.short: An assessment of whether a health system should pay for a medicine, and for which patients.
entries.simpler: The licence says the car is roadworthy; HTA decides whether the company fleet will buy it.

example.text: NICE funds Vazkepa only for secondary prevention with LDL 1.04–2.60 mmol/L, narrower than the EU licence.

entries.notToConfuse: Not regulatory approval: a medicine can be licensed but not reimbursed.

entries.short: EU status (▼) for medicines whose safety is watched especially closely, with extra encouragement to report side effects.
entries.simpler: A 'new driver' sticker: nothing is wrong, but everyone keeps a closer eye.

example.text: Vazkepa carries the black triangle.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a warning that the medicine is unsafe.

entries.short: A trial in which chance decides who gets the medicine and who gets the comparison.
entries.simpler: Tossing a coin for each patient, so the two groups start out alike and only the treatment differs.

example.text: JUPITER randomised 17,802 people to rosuvastatin 20 mg or placebo.

entries.notToConfuse: Not an observational study, where people choose (or are chosen for) treatment.

entries.short: A dummy treatment that looks like the medicine but contains no active drug.
entries.simpler: A decoy, so that expectations affect both groups equally.

example.text: REDUCE-IT's placebo contained light mineral oil; whether that oil was truly inert is still debated.

entries.notToConfuse: Not always perfectly inert, especially for oil capsules.

entries.short: Whatever the medicine is compared against: placebo or another active treatment.
entries.simpler: The yardstick. A result only means something once you know what it was measured against.

example.text: Against glipizide, dapagliflozin lowered HbA1c by the same 0.52 points; against placebo it was a 0.66-point difference.

entries.notToConfuse: Not always placebo: a head-to-head trial uses an active comparator.

entries.short: Neither patients nor investigators know who received which treatment.
entries.simpler: A blind tasting: nobody knows which glass is which, so expectations can't tilt the verdict.

example.text: TECOS was double-blind; patients and doctors didn't know who had sitagliptin.

entries.notToConfuse: Not open-label, where everyone knows.

entries.short: Everyone in the trial knows who is getting what.
entries.simpler: A tasting with the labels showing.

example.text: RACING was open-label, which makes softer outcomes more vulnerable to bias.

entries.notToConfuse: Not automatically worthless: hard outcomes like death are less affected than symptoms.

entries.short: The single main result a trial names in advance to decide whether it succeeded.
entries.simpler: The finish line drawn before the race starts.

example.text: DECLARE had two primary endpoints; the heart-attack/stroke one wasn't superior, the heart-failure one was.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a secondary endpoint, which can only support or question the main answer.

entries.short: Several kinds of event counted together as one outcome.
entries.simpler: Counting 'any car problem' instead of just 'engine failure': more events, but check which problem drives the total.

example.text: DECLARE's heart-failure/CV-death composite improved (HR 0.83), driven by hospitalisations (HR 0.73), not deaths (HR 0.98).

entries.notToConfuse: Not every component improving: always look inside.

entries.short: A composite of major heart and vessel events; the number of components varies by trial.
entries.simpler: A shopping basket of heart events. Always read the label to see what's inside.

example.text: CLEAR Outcomes' MACE-4 (CV death, heart attack, stroke, revascularisation): 11.7% vs 13.3%.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a fixed definition: 3-point, 4-point and 5-point MACE differ.

entries.short: A lab measure accepted in place of outcomes patients care about.
entries.simpler: Checking the fuel gauge instead of whether you reached your destination.

example.text: Fenofibrate lowers triglycerides 40–55%, yet ACCORD-Lipid didn't show fewer heart events.

entries.notToConfuse: Not proof of clinical benefit: a marker can move without outcomes following.

entries.short: The plain difference in event rates between groups, in percentage points.
entries.simpler: If rain falls on 22 of 100 days without an umbrella app and 17 with it, the absolute gain is 5 dry days.

example.text: REDUCE-IT: 22.0% vs 17.2%, an absolute reduction of 4.8 percentage points.

entries.notToConfuse: Not relative risk reduction, which expresses the same difference as a share of the comparator rate.

entries.short: The difference in event rates expressed as a share of the comparator's rate.
entries.simpler: A '25% off' label: impressive, but 25% of what?

example.text: HOPE-3: 4.8% → 3.7% is about 24% relative, but only 1.1 points absolute.

entries.notToConfuse: Not absolute risk: a big relative cut of a small risk can be a tiny absolute gain.

entries.short: How often events happened on the treatment compared with the comparator, over the trial.
entries.simpler: Comparing how often two cars break down per year of driving: 0.75 means 25% fewer breakdowns.

example.text: REDUCE-IT: HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.68–0.83), i.e. about 25% fewer major events.

entries.notToConfuse: Not absolute risk: HR 0.75 can mean 22%→17% or 2%→1.5%.

entries.short: The range of values the trial's data are compatible with.
entries.simpler: A weather forecast range: '18–24 °C', not exactly 21. If the range for a hazard ratio includes 1.0, 'no effect' is still possible.

example.text: TECOS: HR 0.98 (0.88–1.09) includes 1.0, so no effect on heart events either way.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the range where 95% of patients' results fall.

entries.short: How surprising the result would be if the treatment truly had no effect; below 0.05 is the usual bar.
entries.simpler: How odd it would be to flip 9 heads in 10 tosses with a fair coin.

example.text: DECLARE MACE superiority p = 0.172, so later endpoints were only 'nominal'.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the probability that the drug works, and not a measure of how big the effect is.

entries.short: A result unlikely enough under chance alone to count as a real difference, usually p < 0.05.
entries.simpler: A signal loud enough to stand out from background noise.

example.text: ACCORD-Lipid's main result (HR 0.92, CI 0.79–1.08) was not statistically significant.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the same as clinically important: a tiny effect can be significant in a huge trial.

entries.short: How many people need treating, for a stated time, to prevent one event: 100 ÷ absolute risk reduction.
entries.simpler: How many tickets you'd buy to win once.

example.text: REDUCE-IT: 100 ÷ 4.8 ≈ 21 people for about 4.9 years to prevent one event (calculated).

entries.notToConfuse: Not comparable across trials with different patients, follow-up and placebos.

entries.short: A test of whether a treatment is not worse than a comparator by more than a limit set in advance.
entries.simpler: Proving the new route isn't more than 5 minutes slower, not that it's faster.

example.text: TECOS: upper CI 1.09, below the margin of 1.3, so no extra heart harm was shown.

entries.notToConfuse: Not superiority: passing non-inferiority doesn't mean the drug is better.

entries.short: Results for a slice of trial participants; an interaction test checks whether the effect truly differs there.
entries.simpler: Looking only at the left-handed players in a team's season stats: interesting, but small samples mislead.

example.text: ACCORD-Lipid's high-TG/low-HDL subgroup did better, but the interaction p was 0.057.

entries.notToConfuse: Not proof on its own; consistent with the whole trial is not the same as proven in the subgroup.

entries.short: An analysis chosen after the data had been seen.
entries.simpler: Drawing the target around the arrow after it lands.

example.text: The EU Crestor SmPC describes JUPITER through post-hoc higher-risk analyses, not its overall result.

entries.notToConfuse: Not prespecified: post-hoc findings generate hypotheses rather than confirm them.

entries.short: Everyone is analysed in the group they were randomised to, whether or not they took the tablets.
entries.simpler: Judging a diet plan by everyone who signed up, not just those who stuck to it.

example.text: TECOS reported HR 0.98 with an ITT CI of 0.89–1.08 and a per-protocol CI of 0.88–1.09.

entries.notToConfuse: Not per-protocol, which only counts those who followed the plan closely.

entries.short: A trial halted by its independent monitoring committee because benefit (or futility) already looks clear.
entries.simpler: Calling a match at half-time: the lead may be real, but the final score might have been closer.

example.text: DAPA-CKD stopped early for efficacy; STRENGTH stopped for futility.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a guarantee of the effect size: stopping for benefit tends to overstate it.

entries.short: Total follow-up time added across participants; used to express event rates fairly.
entries.simpler: Like counting kilometres driven, not just cars: 100 people for 2 years = 200 person-years.

example.text: DAPA-HF: 11.6 vs 15.6 events per 100 patient-years.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the number of patients.

entries.short: A single estimate combined from several trials.
entries.simpler: Averaging many weather stations to see the regional trend.

example.text: CTT: across 26 statin trials, about 22% fewer major vascular events per 1 mmol/L lower LDL.

entries.notToConfuse: Not stronger than its inputs: pooling different molecules or designs can mislead.

entries.short: A trial that regulators relied on to approve a medicine or an indication.
entries.simpler: The decisive match of a season.

example.text: REDUCE-IT is Vazkepa's single pivotal trial.

entries.notToConfuse: Not every published trial about a medicine.

entries.short: A lead-in period before randomisation, e.g. on placebo, to check adherence or wash out other drugs.
entries.simpler: A trial lap before the real race.

example.text: JUPITER used a four-week placebo run-in to select reliable tablet-takers.

entries.notToConfuse: Not part of the comparison itself.

entries.short: Cholesterol carried in low-density lipoprotein particles; the fraction most closely tied to artery disease.
entries.simpler: The delivery trucks that can crash into artery walls and leave cargo behind.

example.text: Rosuvastatin 10 mg lowered LDL about 52% vs 7% on placebo in the SmPC's dose table.

entries.notToConfuse: Not 'bad cholesterol' as a substance: it's the carrier particle that matters.

entries.short: Cholesterol carried in high-density particles that move cholesterol away from the arteries.
entries.simpler: The clean-up crew. More crew doesn't always mean a cleaner street.

example.text: Fenofibrate raises HDL 10–30%, yet raising HDL hasn't reliably cut heart events.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a treatment target in itself under current guidelines.

entries.short: Fats the body stores and carries in the blood as fuel.
entries.simpler: The fuel in the tank, as opposed to cholesterol, which is building material.

example.text: Vazkepa lowered triglycerides 18%, but the SmPC says that explains only a minor part of its benefit.

entries.notToConfuse: Not cholesterol: different molecule, different drugs.

entries.short: Total cholesterol minus HDL: all the cholesterol in potentially artery-clogging particles.
entries.simpler: All the trucks except the clean-up crew.

example.text: Pravafenix's pivotal trial measured non-HDL: −14.1% vs −6.1% with pravastatin alone.

entries.notToConfuse: Not LDL alone: it also counts VLDL and remnants.

entries.short: The protein carried once on every artery-clogging particle, so it counts the particles.
entries.simpler: Counting the trucks rather than weighing their cargo.

example.text: Bempedoic acid lowers apoB as well as LDL.

entries.notToConfuse: Not apoA1, the main protein of HDL.

entries.short: Disease caused by fatty build-up in the arteries: heart attack, stroke, narrowed leg arteries.
entries.simpler: Rust inside the pipes.

example.text: 71% of REDUCE-IT patients had established cardiovascular disease.

entries.notToConfuse: Not heart failure or rhythm problems, which can have other causes.

entries.short: Primary: preventing a first event. Secondary: preventing another event after one has happened.
entries.simpler: Fitting a smoke alarm before any fire vs after the kitchen already burned once.

example.text: NICE funds Vazkepa only for secondary prevention.

entries.notToConfuse: Not about treatment order (first-line vs second-line).

entries.short: Being unable to take a statin, or an adequate statin dose, because of side effects.
entries.simpler: Being allergic to the standard tool, so you need a different one.

example.text: CLEAR Outcomes enrolled 13,970 statin-intolerant patients; 23% still took a very low statin dose.

entries.notToConfuse: Not one fixed definition: each trial wrote its own rule.

entries.short: A blood test reflecting average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months.
entries.simpler: A three-month average on a fitness tracker rather than today's step count.

example.text: Sitagliptin lowered HbA1c about 0.7 points vs placebo when added to metformin.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a single blood-sugar reading.

entries.short: A lab estimate of how much blood the kidneys filter per minute; it guides dosing.
entries.simpler: The flow rate of the body's water filter.

example.text: Don't start dapagliflozin below GFR 25; an early, expected eGFR 'dip' of about 4 points isn't damage.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the same as creatinine itself, which is one input to the estimate.

entries.short: Blood sugar falling too low, causing shakiness, sweating, confusion or worse.
entries.simpler: Running the tank below empty.

example.text: Versus glipizide: hypoglycaemia 3.5% vs 40.8%.

entries.notToConfuse: Not usually caused by SGLT2 or DPP-4 inhibitors alone; sulphonylureas and insulin are the main culprits.

entries.short: A medicine that must be converted in the body before it works.
entries.simpler: A flat-pack chair: useless until assembled.

example.text: Bempedoic acid is activated by ACSVL1, an enzyme found mainly in the liver.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a weaker drug: once activated it acts normally.

entries.short: The time for blood levels of a medicine to fall by half.
entries.simpler: How long it takes a cup of coffee to cool halfway.

example.text: EPA's half-life is about 89 hours; sitagliptin's about 12.4 hours.

entries.notToConfuse: Not how long the medicine's effect lasts.

entries.short: The share of a dose that reaches the bloodstream.
entries.simpler: How much of a parcel actually arrives after the courier loses some on the way.

example.text: Only about 20% of a rosuvastatin dose reaches the circulation.

entries.notToConfuse: Not potency or effect.

entries.short: Total exposure to a medicine in the blood over time.
entries.simpler: Total rainfall over a day, not the heaviest shower.

example.text: Ciclosporin raises rosuvastatin AUC about 7-fold, which is why the combination is contraindicated.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the peak level (Cmax).

entries.short: Liver enzymes that break down many medicines; blocking them is a common cause of interactions.
entries.simpler: The recycling plant: jam one line and other loads pile up.

example.text: Fenofibrate isn't processed by CYP3A4, removing one interaction route with simvastatin.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the only interaction route: transporters matter too.

entries.short: A protein that moves medicines into or out of cells; blocking it can raise drug levels.
entries.simpler: Doors and pumps in the cell wall: block a door and the drug piles up outside.

example.text: Bempedoic acid blocks OAT2 in the kidney, nudging creatinine and uric acid up.

entries.notToConfuse: Not an enzyme: transporters move drugs, enzymes break them down.

entries.short: An unwanted effect reasonably linked to a medicine; the SmPC groups them by frequency (common = 1 in 100 to 1 in 10).
entries.simpler: An unwanted passenger: the SmPC tells you how often they board.

example.text: Genital infections: 5.5% vs 0.6% on placebo, listed as 'common'.

entries.notToConfuse: Not every adverse event in a trial: events are counted regardless of cause; reactions are judged linked.

entries.short: Monitoring a medicine's safety after it's on the market.
entries.simpler: Keeping the smoke detectors switched on after the house is built.

example.text: The 2009–2011 fibrate referral changed use on benefit grounds; pharmacovigilance covers efficacy questions too.

entries.notToConfuse: Not only about side effects: it reviews the benefit–risk balance.

entries.short: The EU's single assessment of all companies' periodic safety reports for one substance.
entries.simpler: A combined annual check-up for every brand of the same medicine.

example.text: PSUSAs added bullous pemphigoid (2015) and thrombocytopenia (2018) to Januvia's label.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a new trial: it reviews reports and data already collected.

entries.short: A document listing a medicine's important risks and how each is minimised and studied.
entries.simpler: A risk register for one medicine: known hazards, suspected hazards, and blind spots.

example.text: Vazkepa's RMP lists bleeding with antithrombotics and AF as important identified risks.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the SmPC warnings list: a risk can stay in the SmPC after leaving the RMP.

entries.short: New information suggesting a medicine may cause an effect, strong enough to need checking.
entries.simpler: Smoke, before anyone has found the fire.

example.text: A 2023 PRAC signal led to myasthenia warnings for all statins.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a confirmed side effect: many signals are ruled out.

entries.short: Severe muscle breakdown that can damage the kidneys.
entries.simpler: Muscle cells bursting and clogging the kidney's filters.

example.text: Rare with rosuvastatin, but reported more often above 20 mg and with interacting drugs.

entries.notToConfuse: Not ordinary muscle aches (myalgia), which are common and harmless by comparison.

entries.short: Statements of fact one party makes in the contract; if one proves untrue, the other may claim.
entries.simpler: The seller's signed fact sheet about the business. If a fact turns out false, the fact sheet is what you sue on.

example.text: In the module: breach of a rep is the most common indemnity trigger.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a covenant, which is a promise to do or not do something in the future.

entries.short: Wording that limits a rep to what the seller actually knew, e.g. 'to the Seller's knowledge'.
entries.simpler: 'As far as I know, the roof doesn't leak' is a much weaker promise than 'the roof doesn't leak'.

example.text: In the module: knowledge qualifiers narrow what counts as a breach, shifting unknown risk back to the buyer.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the same as a materiality qualifier, which limits a rep to things that matter enough.

entries.short: A clause that ignores 'material' qualifiers in reps when calculating breach or loss for indemnity purposes.
entries.simpler: Removing the 'only if it's serious' filter once you're counting the damage, so small breaches still add up.

example.text: In the module: a scrape stops 'material' from being counted twice, once in the rep and again in the basket.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the basket itself: the scrape decides what counts; the basket decides when you can recover.

entries.short: A contractual promise by one party to cover the other's losses from specified events.
entries.simpler: A promise to pay the bill if certain things go wrong, written down before anything has gone wrong.

example.text: In the module: the clause names who indemnifies whom, for what, and within which limits.

entries.notToConfuse: Not insurance, although it does a similar job: here the counterparty, not an insurer, pays.

entries.short: The indemnifying party pays; the indemnified party is protected and claims.
entries.simpler: The guarantor and the person being guaranteed.

example.text: In the module: the indemnifying party usually wants control of the defence; the indemnified party wants a say in settlement.

entries.notToConfuse: Not fixed by role in the deal: buyer and seller can each be either, depending on the clause.

entries.short: A claim between the two contracting parties themselves, e.g. buyer against seller for a breached rep.
entries.simpler: A dispute inside the family, with no outsider involved.

example.text: In the module: direct and third-party claims run on different procedures, and are often conflated.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a third-party claim, where an outsider sues first and the indemnity passes the cost on.

entries.short: A claim by an outsider (patient, competitor, regulator) against the indemnified party that the indemnity may cover.
entries.simpler: Someone outside the deal knocks on the door, and the contract decides who answers and who pays.

example.text: In the module: the first 30 days after a third-party claim arrives decide a lot: notice, timing, defence.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a direct claim between the deal parties.

entries.short: The formal notification the indemnified party must give, with content and deadlines set by the contract.
entries.simpler: Reporting a car accident to your insurer: late or incomplete reports can cost you cover.

example.text: In the module: what happens when notice is late or defective, and whether the indemnifying party must show prejudice.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the claim itself: notice starts the procedure; it doesn't prove the loss.

entries.short: Who runs the response to a third-party claim: picks counsel, sets strategy, pays.
entries.simpler: Who holds the steering wheel when the car you both care about is in trouble.

example.text: In the module: the most consequential and least understood procedural term.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the same as paying: one party can fund the defence while the other controls it, or vice versa.

entries.short: A clause requiring one party's agreement before the other settles a third-party claim.
entries.simpler: Neither driver can sell the shared car without the other's signature.

example.text: In the module: where interests genuinely diverge, e.g. a settlement that's cheap for the payer but admits fault for the protected party.

entries.notToConfuse: Not control of defence: you can control the defence yet still need consent to settle.

entries.short: The obligation to give the other side the documents, people and access needed to handle a claim.
entries.simpler: Sharing the keys and the paperwork so whoever is driving can actually drive.

example.text: In the module: practical cooperation during a live claim, and its tension with privilege.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a waiver of privilege, which needs to be protected separately.

entries.short: Protection keeping certain lawyer–client communications confidential from opponents and courts.
entries.simpler: A sealed envelope that the other side in a dispute can't open, unless you open it yourself.

example.text: In the module: how privilege survives, or doesn't, when two parties coordinate a defence.

entries.notToConfuse: Not general confidentiality: an NDA doesn't create privilege.

entries.short: Losses that flow naturally and immediately from the breach.
entries.simpler: The broken window itself, not the burglary it later allowed.

example.text: In the module: what is actually recoverable once a claim succeeds.

entries.notToConfuse: Not consequential damages, which are further removed and often excluded.

entries.short: Losses one step removed from the breach, such as lost profits or lost opportunities.
entries.simpler: Not the broken window, but the sales you lost while the shop was closed for repairs.

example.text: In the module: why consequential damages exclusions are negotiated so hard.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a fixed legal category everywhere: what counts as 'consequential' varies by jurisdiction and drafting.

entries.short: An exception that takes a matter outside a general rule or limit.
entries.simpler: A 'except for…' line that punches a hole in a fence.

example.text: In the module: fraud and fundamental reps are typical carve-outs from caps and exclusions.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a separate indemnity, though specific indemnities often sit in carve-outs.

entries.short: The maximum total amount the indemnifying party can be made to pay.
entries.simpler: The ceiling on the bill, however bad things get.

example.text: In the module: caps, baskets and de minimis work together as one financial architecture.

entries.notToConfuse: Not a basket, which sets the floor before recovery starts.

entries.short: A loss threshold that must be reached before indemnity claims can be paid.
entries.simpler: Worked illustration: €1m basket, €1.2m loss. A tipping basket pays €1.2m from the first euro; a deductible pays only €0.2m above the threshold.

example.text: In the module: the deductible vs tipping basket distinction changes outcomes materially.

entries.notToConfuse: Not de minimis: de minimis filters individual small claims; the basket applies to the aggregate.

entries.short: A minimum size below which individual claims are ignored, and often don't count towards the basket either.
entries.simpler: A shop that won't process returns under €5.

example.text: In the module: de minimis claims can quietly erode a basket if they don't count towards it.

entries.notToConfuse: Not the basket: de minimis works claim by claim; the basket works on the total.

entries.short: How long reps and indemnities remain claimable after closing.
entries.simpler: The warranty period on the deal itself: after it expires, you can't claim.

example.text: In the module: how claim timing interacts with survival, and why fundamental reps survive longer.
